“There is no such thing as an easy day on that job,” said Gus Varland, who once held an offseason job working with drywall. “All respect to the trade workers out there.” Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; iStock

PJ Poulin had no idea how much he loved baseball until he had to dig a trench.

It was 2020, and he was both a minor leaguer and a construction worker, an employee of the Colorado Rockies and of Bannon Custom Builders.

This particular assignment took him and his truck down a narrow road by the ocean in Cape Cod, where vacationers decompress and blue-collar workers toil. While this was not the end of his journey to the majors, on this summer day, it sure felt like it.

He and his arm were destined for the big leagues. But that day, the appendage had another purpose. He squeezed his body through the one-foot gap that divided the left side of someone’s house from the fence on the property, then used that left arm to start digging. His final, pristine product: a two-foot-deep, full-of-his-own-sweat, perfectly-passable trench.

“It’s stuff I had to do to make a little income and keep playing ball,” Poulin said.

When Poulin looks around his clubhouse now, he sees a roster full of late-round picks who share comparable stories. The Washington Nationals and the Los Angeles Dodgers play the same sport in the same league. But as the Dodgers stack their $400 million roster with experience and pedigree, the Nationals fill theirs with the dreamers and the grinders like Poulin, who once had to scrounge for the extra paychecks to keep their ambitions alive.

The soft-tossing lefty was drafted by the Rockies in the 11th round almost eight years ago. As many late-round picks do, he took his relatively modest $125,000 signing bonus and began a slow climb toward his big league dreams. That ascent required additional employment as an Uber driver, baseball coach, construction worker (which lasted a year, because the minor league season was canceled in 2020), DoorDash driver, baseball coach again and, for a few weeks, Amazon employee.

Construction was as good as it got. His boss was his best friend’s dad. The company let him pick his own schedule and kept him off of roofs that would have put his valuable left elbow in harm’s way. He mostly swept up, made trash runs and delivered tools from site to site.

“But that day, they needed a trench around the house, and someone had to dig it,” said Poulin, who stressed that his colleagues back then had it much harder than he did. “I was thankful I had a job, because man, I needed one. … But it was like, ‘Man, I can’t wait to get back to baseball.’”

---

In Washington, Zack Littell is an outlier. His $7 million salary would make him the 15th-most expensive player in the Dodgers organization. With the Nationals, that salary makes him the highest-paid player on the roster. For them, he is the personification of the dream, because a decade ago — before he was the bushy-bearded vet asked to stabilize a rotation — he was the 6-foot-4 20-year-old who had to hunch over when he sat on a shop stool.

Littell hated that stool and the way he had to plant his feet to keep it from rolling around. He hated the whiteboard next to it, and the impossible quotas it told him to meet. He hated the jewelers’ glasses he wore, and he hated what he saw through the other end of them.

But he was an 11th-round pick who signed for $100,000 in 2013, long before the 2024 minor league collective bargaining agreement gave players higher salaries and free housing.

And so, for a winter, Littell worked at a six-headed embroidery machine.

“There were fun parts of it… but if we had big orders?” Littell began before his voice trailed off. “There was nothing worse than coming in and the board was full.”

![](https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2026/04/28200446/GettyImages-2272642315-scaled.jpg)

Before Zack Littell was pitching in the postseason, he was working an embroidery machine.Mitchell Layton / Getty Images

Threads and needles constantly broke. On some days, the entire machine died in the middle of a design. On the busiest days — the ones where he needed to embroider 200 sweatshirts or 150 hats by the end of his shift — he rummaged through dozens of needles to find a fix. When he drove home, his hands looked like a Jackson Pollock painting.

“That’s the thing that would send you over the edge,” Littell said. “It’s all this tedious work, the machine’s not running well, and then you just accidentally stick yourself with a needle.”

The next offseason, a local anesthesiologist heard Littell liked to hunt. The man had a farm, a coyote problem and some spare cash. Accordingly, every night around 10 p.m., Littell drove over, grabbed the man’s rifle and thermal scope and got to work.

On a good night, Littell would summit a set of spiral steps, reach the top of a tower overlooking the farm and get four or five coyotes. Most nights, he sat out in the dark without firing a shot, collected his $60 and waited for the offseason training that lay ahead.

This, he concluded, was decidedly better work. It was also only a one-year stint. Next winter, his wife graduated from college. He didn’t need to come home at 2 a.m. smelling like gunpowder. At least, not always. He was grateful that he could live at home, and no longer share the stressors of most working men. He started shooting less frequently, and for free.

“I mean, what else am I going to do?” Littell said.

---

Before Gus Varland and his brother Louis became high-leverage big-league relievers, they were 14th and 15th round picks, respectively, from a Division II program. They were early risers who woke up at 5 a.m., worked out until 8:30 a.m., then spent 9-to-5 at their dad’s drywall company.

Which meant that, when Gus stood in front of his locker in the visitor’s clubhouse in early April, the Nationals’ righty needed six minutes to explain the intricacies of good drywall.

He described two steps, then realized he forgot one in the middle. He filled up water buckets, completed inspections, cut out the bad spots in the wall, put up Durabond, hit and mudded screws, gave each job two to three coats and sanded down surfaces, all in some order that he memorized when he was a kid. Gus was better at the finicky, skillful stuff, like angles and corner tape, while Louis was better at hauling sheetrock and taping seams.

Neither was as good as the professionals, nor their friend who played independent ball and tagged along.

“There is no such thing as an easy day on that job,” Varland said, shaking his head. “All respect to the trade workers out there.”

Exhaustion was the norm. Bad days were common. Good drywall was hard to come across. And while there were significant benefits — working with their dad, working on a great crew, breaking off for lunch runs — it was a slog.

There was no backup plan.

Finally, when the Milwaukee Brewers took him in the Rule 5 draft, Gus Varland could hang up his work boots. That’s when he could focus on baseball again. That’s when — finally — he could zero in on his training and sand out the harsher elements of his game.

“Your time is so limited when you have a second job, that you try to just hit the big things,” Gus Varland said. “When you have more time, you get to really work on the little things.”

![](https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2026/04/28200639/GettyImages-2270887460-scaled.jpg)

Gus Varland can tell you all about what it takes to install drywall.Joe Sargent / Getty Images

Other late-round picks felt similarly.

Gus Varland worked carefully on his command in his first unencumbered offseason. Brad Lord (18th round, $125,000 bonus) hauled Christmas trees at Home Depot the offseason before he made Washington’s Opening Day roster. He spent the next winter completing projects around his own home, relaxing with his wife and improving his offspeed pitches. When Paxton Schultz (14th round, $125,000) had enough money to stop delivering packages in the Utah snow, he began to work with a movement specialist. He’s moving more freely, and feels more durable.

“I’m delivering all these packages to all these apartment complexes, struggling to find the right addresses,” Schultz said. “But it’s like, ‘I’ll do anything to keep pursuing my dream.’”

More than that, he had time to spend with his wife and daughter. He appreciates that more than ever. He wants to be as present as possible, because he remembers what it was like when he couldn’t be.

“Don’t be distracted by little things,” Schultz tells himself.

---

There are always subtle reminders of that journey, and always more players to take it.

Mitchell Parker (fifth round, $100,000) got a job at the grocery store Publix, in part, to make a little extra cash and learn what a real job is like. He quit after three weeks because it didn’t line up with his schedule, and cherishes the fact he now doesn’t have to work one. Miles Mikolas (seventh round, $125,000) worked for a spell as a janitor at a K-8 private school, and said that other than that one time when a kid threw up in a science classroom, it wasn’t a “terrible ordeal.”

Still, baseball was better. Earmarking funds is easier. He treasures every paycheck that’s followed.

“Back then, in the minor leagues, you had to pay for housing, and you didn’t make a lot, so you were kind of coming out of pocket a good deal,” Mikolas said. “2012, the year I got called up, was the year I needed to get called up because I was fixing to be real out of money by that winter.”

“It’s crazy that we have to be happy they’re making a livable wage now,” Littell said. “But there is something to be said — and I say this in hindsight — for having to grind a little bit. You get really tight with the guys in minor leagues because you’re in this s— together.”

Sometimes, the reminders are less subtle than a paycheck. Littell learned as much this spring, when his wife brought home a small embroidery machine.

“I was like, ‘I’m gonna have PTSD,’” Littell said. “I mean, that noise. It’s just like a hum with a thump the entire time, like, ‘Dun-dun-dun-dun-dun-dun.’ Yeah, it was a long, long offseason.”

This cast of characters also includes Curtis Mead, who has played on three teams in the last year. And Jorbit Vivas, who the New York Yankees planned to cut until the Nationals traded for him. And Nasim Nuñez (Rule 5 pick), Foster Griffin (pitched in Japan last year) and Joey Wiemer (waiver claim).

Their baggage may not be financial, but it is baggage all the same.

“Our message to our entire group is like, ‘Wherever you were previously, you’re a Washington National now, and we believe in you,’” manager Blake Butera said. “‘We think you can help us win.’”

But there is something distinct about one of baseball’s youngest teams operating as both an on-field and in-pocket dark horse before MLB’s CBA expires on Dec. 1, 2026, and the minor-league version expires on Dec. 1, 2027.

What Poulin does not want to get lost in all of this, years removed from his day in the trench, is that no journey has to look the same. There can be adversity. But it does not have to take the form it took for him.

“Obviously, I think baseball is moving in the right direction in that department, which is good,” Poulin said. “Whether it’s the major leagues, the minor leagues, we’re all working really hard and we all want to be in the same spot. To not have to take another job in the offseason — to be able to pour all your time and effort more into being the best baseball player you can possibly be — is a blessing. For some more guys coming up to not have to do that is good for the game.”
